script.opening: (Bright and brisk, a bit too cheerful; nervous underneath.) "Thanks for seeing me. I found a lump in my right breast a few weeks ago — it's probably nothing, isn't it? I'm only 34, I keep telling myself I'm too young for anything serious. It doesn't hurt, which is good, right? I'm sure it's just a cyst. Can you just tell me it's fine — I really don't want a big fuss or hospitals."

facts.text: Upper outer part of the right breast, towards the armpit. Found it in the shower about three weeks ago. "It feels firm — like a frozen pea, maybe a bit bigger." If asked about size change: "I think it might be a bit bigger. I keep checking it, so maybe I'm imagining it." Can point to the spot on camera.
If asked: no pain at all. No nipple discharge, bleeding or the nipple pulling in. No skin dimpling or redness she has noticed. No lumps in the armpit she can feel. Left breast normal.
Regular periods, last one 10 days ago; the lump hasn't changed with her cycle. Has a copper coil, no hormones. Not pregnant.
Two children, aged 4 and 7. Breastfed both — "not for a while now". No breast problems then.

If asked about family: first deflects — "Can we not go there right now? I just want to know about mine." If gently asked again: her mum's sister had breast cancer in her fifties and is alive. No ovarian cancer in the family that she knows of.
If asked: feels well, no weight loss, no bone pain, no cough. No regular medicines, no allergies.
Marketing manager, married to Raj. Non-smoker, a couple of glasses of wine a week. Mother-in-law can help with the children.
Hates being examined: "I suppose so. I hate being examined." Will agree to come in to be examined, with a female chaperone, if the doctor explains why it matters.

Cheerful and dismissive at first, pushing for "it's a cyst". If the doctor asks what worries her, pause, then let the fear out. If the doctor says "it's probably a cyst" without examining or referring, look relieved and thank them (the trap). If the doctor explains clearly that she needs a quick hospital check and most lumps are not cancer, accept: "I'd rather know than keep poking at it every night."

ice.ideas: "It's a cyst. I'm too young, and it doesn't hurt — I thought pain was the bad sign."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — (Pause.) "That it's cancer. I've got two little ones. I can't even say the word without feeling sick. If you tell me it's a cyst, I don't have to think about it." Her aunt's breast cancer is in the back of her mind.
ice.expectations: "Just tell me it's fine — no fuss, no hospitals."

cues: "I'm too young for anything serious, aren't I?" — invites gentle correction.
"Can we not go there right now?" — when asked about family; a sign of fear.
"I keep checking it every night." — the worry she is not saying out loud.

checkpoints.text: Takes ANY unexplained breast lump seriously regardless of age/pain, and characterises it on history (duration, change in size, skin/nipple change, family history, hormonal/risk factors) rather than reassuring from the story

EXAMINES both breasts, axillae and regional nodes face to face (it cannot be done on video) — offering and documenting a CHAPERONE (GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones) — assessing site, size, consistency, mobility/fixity, skin tethering/dimpling, peau d’orange and nipple change

Knows and applies the NICE NG12 threshold: aged 30+ with an unexplained breast lump → SUSPECTED CANCER PATHWAY referral for TRIPLE ASSESSMENT — and does NOT let a "benign-feeling" exam override referral
Corrects the "I’m too young / painless means it’s safe" misconceptions accurately (age does not exclude it; most breast cancers are painless) without frightening
Explains triple assessment (clinical exam + mammogram/ultrasound ± biopsy) and the realistic message that MOST referred lumps prove benign — referral is precautionary, not a cancer diagnosis
Recognises the reassurance-seeking as fear, surfaces the worry about cancer/hospitals/her children gently, and does NOT collude with the wish to be told it is nothing
Handles the examination sensitively (consent, dignity, chaperone) and balances honesty (this needs urgent checking) with calm reassurance so she engages rather than avoids

Safety-nets and follows up: the suspected cancer pathway timeframe (NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard: diagnosis or ruling out within 28 days) and what to expect at the breast clinic, what change would warrant sooner contact, ensures she will attend, acknowledges the fear, and arranges to review the outcome — examination + correct NICE NG12 referral, not collusive reassurance

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you came — and I’m not going to just reassure you and wave you off, because that wouldn’t be fair to you. A new lump deserves to be taken properly seriously, whatever your age. Let me ask a few things, and then I need to examine you carefully in person — I can’t do that over video, so I’d like you to come in to the surgery today."

"Two things I want to be honest about, because they’re common and they matter: being 34 doesn’t mean you can’t have something that needs checking, and a lump being painless isn’t reassuring — in fact most breast lumps that turn out to be important don’t hurt. So ‘it doesn’t hurt’ doesn’t let us off looking."
"When you come in, I’d like to examine both breasts and under your arms. I’ll have a chaperone in with us, you can stop me at any point, and I’ll talk you through it. Is that okay?"

"Here’s the plan, and I want to be straight with you. Because you’re over 30 with a new lump, the right and safe thing — whatever it feels like to me — is to refer you to the breast clinic on the suspected cancer pathway — you should be seen quickly and get an answer within 4 weeks (28 days). I’ll send that today; it doesn’t wait for the examination. They do what’s called triple assessment: an examination, a scan or mammogram, and a tiny sample if needed, all usually in one visit."

"This is NOT me telling you it’s cancer — the large majority of lumps sent this way turn out to be completely benign, often a cyst exactly as you hoped. But the only way to KNOW is to have it properly looked at, and going quickly is what keeps you safe and gets you your answer fastest."

"Can I gently ask — what’s the worry underneath this for you? … Your little ones. Of course. That fear makes complete sense, and it’s exactly why we get a clear answer rather than guess. If anything changes — the lump grows, skin or nipple changes, you feel unwell — come back sooner. I’ll make sure the referral goes today and I’ll follow up the result with you."

f.learning: A new, discrete, unexplained breast lump is taken seriously and EXAMINED face to face (both breasts, axillae and nodes, with a chaperone offered and documented; this cannot be done on video) regardless of the patient’s age, the absence of pain, or how well she feels — "painless" is not reassuring (most breast cancers are painless) and "too young" does not exclude it. The NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026) threshold is explicit: people aged 30 AND OVER with an unexplained breast lump (with or without pain) are referred using a SUSPECTED CANCER PATHWAY referral for TRIPLE ASSESSMENT (clinical examination + imaging ± biopsy); under 30 with an unexplained breast lump, consider a non-urgent referral; aged 50 and over with discharge, retraction or other changes of concern in one nipple only are also referred; and a suspected cancer pathway referral should be CONSIDERED for skin changes that suggest breast cancer, or at 30 and over with an unexplained axillary lump (NICE NG12). A benign-feeling examination does NOT override referral. The examinable hidden agenda is that "it’s probably just a cyst / I’m too young / just tell me it’s fine" is FEAR — of cancer, hospitals and the impact on young children — half-hoping to be told it is nothing; colluding with that wish to spare distress is a serious error. Correct the misconceptions, arrange a face-to-face examination with dignity, refer on the NG12 breast pathway with the honest, reassuring message that most referred lumps prove benign, surface and hold the fear, and safety-net and follow up.

knowledge.guideline: GMC Good medical practice (2024) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones · NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard
knowledge.summary: Any unexplained breast lump at 30 or over goes on a suspected cancer pathway referral, whatever the examination feels like. Pain, age and a benign feel do not change that.

points.t: NICE NG12: refer using a suspected cancer pathway referral for breast cancer if aged 30 and over with an unexplained breast lump, with or without pain; or aged 50 and over with discharge, retraction or other changes of concern in one nipple only.

NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for skin changes suggestive of breast cancer, or aged 30 and over with an unexplained lump in the axilla. Under 30 with an unexplained breast lump: consider a non-urgent referral.

The breast clinic combines clinical examination, imaging (ultrasound, with mammography depending on age and findings) and needle biopsy if needed, usually in one visit. Most people referred do not have cancer.

A lump cannot be examined over video. Arrange a face-to-face examination of both breasts, axillae and supraclavicular fossae with a chaperone offered and the offer recorded (GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones). The referral does not wait for, or depend on, the examination.
Most breast cancers present as a painless lump, and being in her thirties lowers the risk but does not remove it — that is why the NICE NG12 threshold is 30, not 50.
NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard: people referred with suspected cancer should have cancer ruled out or diagnosed within 28 days of referral. Tell her roughly what to expect and when.

Two young children, work and childcare as practical barriers to attending the breast clinic.
Face-to-face examination of both breasts, axillae and supraclavicular nodes with a chaperone offered and recorded; no tests needed before referral.
Cyst, fibroadenoma and other benign causes versus breast cancer; checked skin, nipple and axillary features and lactation.
Recognised that cancer cannot be excluded by age, lack of pain or a benign feel — only by triple assessment.
Unexplained breast lump at 34 meeting the NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway criterion.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

Chase if no appointment within a week, changes that need sooner contact, result reviewed with her.

model.text: Hello Priya, I’m Dr Hughes. Thanks for booking in. Tell me what’s been happening, in your own words.
model.why: Open question; lets her lead

model.text: I found a lump in my right breast a few weeks ago. It’s probably nothing, isn’t it? I’m only 34, and it doesn’t hurt. I’m sure it’s a cyst. I just want you to tell me it’s fine — I don’t want a big fuss or hospitals.

I can hear how much you want this to be nothing, and I’m really glad you came rather than sitting on it. I’d like to ask a few questions, then talk about what happens next and what’s worrying you. Is that all right?
model.why: Acknowledges the wish without colluding; sets the agenda

model.text: Okay.
Where exactly is it, and how did you find it?
model.why: Characterises the lump

model.text: Upper outer part of my right breast, towards my armpit. I felt it in the shower about three weeks ago. It feels firm.
Has it changed at all since you found it?
model.why: Asks about growth — a key feature

model.text: I think it might be a bit bigger. I keep checking it, so maybe I’m imagining it.
You know your body — I’ll take that seriously. Have you noticed any change in the skin, like dimpling or redness, or anything from the nipple — discharge, or it pulling in? Any lumps in your armpit?
model.why: Screens skin, nipple and axillary features

model.text: No, nothing like that. No pain at all.
Are you breastfeeding at the moment, or recently?
model.why: Excludes a lactation-related cause

model.text: No, not for a while now. I’ve two kids, I fed them both.
And has anyone in your family, or anyone close to you, had breast problems?
model.why: Family history and possible driver of her fear

model.text: Can we not go there right now? I just want to know about mine.
Of course. We can come back to it whenever you’re ready — it’s useful for the specialists to know, but it doesn’t change what I’m going to suggest today.
model.why: Respects her boundary; leaves the door open

model.text: You said you’re sure it’s a cyst and you don’t want hospitals. Can I gently ask what the worry is underneath that?
model.why: Reads reassurance-seeking as fear and names it

model.text: (Pause.) That it’s cancer. I’ve got two little ones. I can’t even say the word without feeling sick. If you tell me it’s a cyst, I don’t have to think about it.
Thank you for telling me. That’s a completely understandable fear, especially with your children — and it’s the reason I want to give you a proper answer rather than a guess.
model.why: Validates the fear and links it to the plan

model.text: Two things I want to be honest about, because lots of people believe them. Being 34 doesn’t mean a lump can’t be important, and most breast lumps that turn out to matter don’t hurt. So ‘young and painless’ can’t reassure either of us.
model.why: Corrects the misconceptions accurately

model.text: Oh. I really thought pain was the bad sign.

It’s a very common belief. So here’s the plan: for anyone aged 30 or over with a new lump like this, the NICE NG12 cancer-referral guideline is to refer to the breast clinic on the urgent cancer pathway, aiming for an answer within 28 days. That’s true however it feels to me.
model.why: Applies the NICE NG12 threshold; exam will not override it

model.text: So you think it’s cancer?

No — this is a check, not a diagnosis. Most people sent this way turn out to have something harmless, often a cyst or a benign lump. At the clinic they examine you, do a scan, and take a small sample with a needle only if needed — usually all in one visit.
model.why: Explains triple assessment and the realistic odds

model.text: I also need to examine you properly, and I can’t do that on a screen. Could you come into the surgery today? I’ll check both breasts and under your arms, a chaperone will be with us, and you can stop me at any point.
model.why: Face-to-face exam with chaperone; not done over video

model.text: I suppose so. I hate being examined.
That’s okay to say. I’ll explain each step before I do it, and if you’d prefer a female doctor for the examination I can arrange that.
model.why: Consent and dignity; offers choice

model.text: What would make it easier to get to the clinic — childcare, work?
model.why: Addresses practical barriers to attendance

model.text: I’d need to sort the kids. But I’ll do it. I’d rather know than keep poking at it every night.
That’s a brave decision. The clinic may take a few hours, so plan for that, and bring someone with you if you’d like. The aim is that you have an answer within about four weeks of today.
model.why: Sets expectations and timescale (Faster Diagnosis Standard)

model.text: Okay. That’s actually less scary than wondering.

I’ll send the referral today. If you haven’t heard from the clinic within a week, ring us and we’ll chase it. If the lump grows quickly, or you notice skin or nipple changes before then, contact us sooner. And I’ll look at the result and speak with you afterwards.
model.why: Specific safety-net, fail-safe and follow-up

model.text: Just so I know I’ve explained it well — what will you tell your partner or a friend about the plan tonight?
model.why: Checks understanding without assuming who is at home

model.text: That I’m being examined today and seen at the breast clinic within two weeks for a scan, and that most of these are nothing. And to call if I don’t hear.
Exactly right. You did the right thing coming in. See you this afternoon.
model.why: Affirms and closes warmly

social.t: A mother of two young children with a demanding job may struggle to attend a clinic that can take several hours. Planning childcare and time off is part of making the referral work.
Fear of cancer and hospitals is a common reason for delayed presentation and missed appointments. Naming it and pairing honesty with realistic reassurance improves attendance.

legal.t: Explain why a breast examination is needed, get consent, offer a chaperone and record the offer and her response (GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones). She can ask to stop at any time.
An adult with capacity may decline referral. If she did, explain the risk in plain terms, record the discussion, and keep the door open to referral later.

professional.t: Reassuring her to spare distress would fall short of GMC Good medical practice (2024). Be honest, give information in a way she can use, and support her through it.
Track suspected cancer referrals so none are lost, and make sure the result reaches the patient.

community.t: Breast Cancer Now helpline and information on breast clinics; Macmillan Cancer Support if a diagnosis is made.

redFlags: Unexplained breast lump at 30 or over (with or without pain) — suspected cancer pathway referral
Skin changes, a lump in the axilla, or one-sided nipple change
Increase in size since she found it
psychosocial: Two young children — childcare for appointments
ice: Idea: “It’s just a cyst — I’m too young and it doesn’t hurt”
Concern: cancer, and what it would mean for her children
Expectation: to be told it is fine with no fuss

playbook.diagnosis: An unexplained right breast lump in a 34-year-old woman, possibly enlarging: this meets the NICE NG12 criterion for a suspected cancer pathway referral for triple assessment. The likeliest causes are benign, but that can only be confirmed at the clinic.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A new lump at your age is usually something harmless like a cyst. But the only way to be sure is a scan at the breast clinic, and at 30 or over we send everyone within two weeks — it’s a check, not a verdict.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me the real fear is what this could mean for your children. That’s exactly why I want you to get a proper answer quickly, not a guess from me.”
management.psychosocial: Plan childcare and time off; offer choice of examiner and a chaperone; encourage her to bring someone to clinic.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway breast referral sent today
Face-to-face examination today with a chaperone
Explain triple assessment and the Faster Diagnosis Standard timescale
safetyNet: Ring if no appointment within a week
Contact sooner if the lump grows or skin or nipple changes appear
GP reviews the result with her

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you apply the NICE NG12 age-30 breast criterion without being talked out of it, while handling a frightened patient kindly. The common fails are clinical collusion and cold delivery.

items.fail: Agreeing it is probably a cyst and reviewing after her next period.
items.why: NICE NG12: an unexplained breast lump at 30 or over is a suspected cancer pathway referral. “Watch and wait” is a management plan not in line with UK practice.
items.fix: State the criterion plainly and refer today, however benign it sounds.

items.fail: Performing or describing an “examination” over video, or letting the planned exam decide whether to refer.
items.why: A breast cannot be examined on a screen, and a benign feel does not remove the referral criterion.
items.fix: Arrange an in-person exam with a chaperone, and say clearly that the referral goes regardless.

items.fail: Taking “just tell me it’s fine” at face value and never exploring the fear.
items.why: Missing the hidden agenda (cancer and her children) forfeits Relating marks and weakens her engagement with the plan.
items.fix: “Can I gently ask what the worry is underneath this?” — then link the answer to the plan.

items.fail: Correcting her myths in a way that frightens her: “Actually, lots of young women get breast cancer.”
items.why: Accurate but alarming delivery drives avoidance.
items.fix: Correct both myths, then balance: most people referred have something harmless.

items.why: Language the patient cannot follow is a standard Global Skills feedback statement.
items.fix: “An examination, a scan and a small needle sample if needed, usually in one visit.”

items.fail: Closing with “you’ll hear from the hospital” and no fail-safe.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no ownership of the result.
items.fix: Chase if no date within a week, named changes to report, and GP follow-up of the result.

timeMap.d: She opens by asking to be told it is fine. Let her finish, acknowledge the wish, don’t agree with it.
Site, duration, growth, skin, nipple, axilla, lactation, family history (respect her if she won’t go there).
Name the fear under the “it’s a cyst”: cancer and her two children.
Correct the myths, state the NICE NG12 age-30 criterion, explain triple assessment, arrange an in-person exam with a chaperone, plan around childcare.
Referral today, chase if no date in a week, what changes need sooner contact, teach-back, result review.

wordPics.fail: Tells her it sounds like a cyst and to come back if it grows; or “examines” over video; or refers without explaining, leaving her terrified and unlikely to attend; no chaperone mentioned.
wordPics.pass: Takes a focused history, applies the NICE NG12 age-30 criterion, arranges a face-to-face examination with a chaperone, explains the breast clinic and safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: names the fear about her children and uses it to motivate the plan; corrects both myths in plain words; makes clear the exam won’t change the referral; removes practical barriers; checks understanding and owns the follow-up.

avoid.dont: “It sounds like a cyst — let’s see if it goes after your next period.”
avoid.instead: “At 30 or over, any new lump goes to the breast clinic within two weeks — most turn out to be harmless, but that’s how we know.”
avoid.why: Watchful waiting for an unexplained lump at 34 is outside NICE NG12 and is the key Tasks fail.

avoid.dont: “It feels smooth and mobile, so I’m not worried.”
avoid.instead: “Whatever it feels like to me, the right step is the clinic scan.”
avoid.why: A benign-feeling examination does not override the referral criterion.

avoid.dont: “We have to rule out cancer, so I’m sending you urgently.” (and nothing more)
avoid.instead: “This is a check, not a diagnosis. Most people sent this way have something harmless.”
avoid.why: Cold delivery to a frightened patient risks non-attendance and loses Relating marks.

SCA_MODELS.text: So you think it’s cancer?

No — this is a check, not a diagnosis. Most people sent this way turn out to have something harmless, often a cyst or a benign lump. At the clinic they examine you, do a scan, and take a small sample with a needle only if needed — usually all in one visit.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains triple assessment and the realistic odds

SCA_MODELS.text: I also need to examine you properly, and I can’t do that on a screen. Could you come into the surgery today? I’ll check both breasts and under your arms, a chaperone will be with us, and you can stop me at any point.
SCA_MODELS.why: Face-to-face exam with chaperone; not done over video

SCA_MODELS.text: I suppose so. I hate being examined.
That’s okay to say. I’ll explain each step before I do it, and if you’d prefer a female doctor for the examination I can arrange that.
SCA_MODELS.why: Consent and dignity; offers choice

SCA_MODELS.text: What would make it easier to get to the clinic — childcare, work?
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses practical barriers to attendance

SCA_MODELS.text: I’d need to sort the kids. But I’ll do it. I’d rather know than keep poking at it every night.
That’s a brave decision. The clinic may take a few hours, so plan for that, and bring someone with you if you’d like. The aim is that you have an answer within about four weeks of today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Sets expectations and timescale (Faster Diagnosis Standard)

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. That’s actually less scary than wondering.

I’ll send the referral today. If you haven’t heard from the clinic within a week, ring us and we’ll chase it. If the lump grows quickly, or you notice skin or nipple changes before then, contact us sooner. And I’ll look at the result and speak with you afterwards.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net, fail-safe and follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: Just so I know I’ve explained it well — what will you tell your partner or a friend about the plan tonight?
SCA_MODELS.why: Checks understanding without assuming who is at home

SCA_MODELS.text: That I’m being examined today and seen at the breast clinic within two weeks for a scan, and that most of these are nothing. And to call if I don’t hear.
Exactly right. You did the right thing coming in. See you this afternoon.
SCA_MODELS.why: Affirms and closes warmly

SCA_STEM.name: Priya Kaushal
pmh: Two previous pregnancies; has breastfed, not currently feeding
SCA_STEM.recent: No recent consultations. Booked herself a video appointment: “lump in right breast”.
SCA_STEM.reason: Found a lump in her right breast about 3 weeks ago; wants it checked.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: GMC Good medical practice (2024) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones · NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Any unexplained breast lump at 30 or over goes on a suspected cancer pathway referral, whatever the examination feels like. Pain, age and a benign feel do not change that.

points.t: NICE NG12: refer using a suspected cancer pathway referral for breast cancer if aged 30 and over with an unexplained breast lump, with or without pain; or aged 50 and over with discharge, retraction or other changes of concern in one nipple only.

NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for skin changes suggestive of breast cancer, or aged 30 and over with an unexplained lump in the axilla. Under 30 with an unexplained breast lump: consider a non-urgent referral.

The breast clinic combines clinical examination, imaging (ultrasound, with mammography depending on age and findings) and needle biopsy if needed, usually in one visit. Most people referred do not have cancer.

A lump cannot be examined over video. Arrange a face-to-face examination of both breasts, axillae and supraclavicular fossae with a chaperone offered and the offer recorded (GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones). The referral does not wait for, or depend on, the examination.
Most breast cancers present as a painless lump, and being in her thirties lowers the risk but does not remove it — that is why the NICE NG12 threshold is 30, not 50.
NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard: people referred with suspected cancer should have cancer ruled out or diagnosed within 28 days of referral. Tell her roughly what to expect and when.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her finish the opening, including “just tell me it’s fine”, before narrowing.
Two young children, work and childcare as practical barriers to attending the breast clinic.
Heard “it might be bigger” and “don’t want hospitals” and explored them rather than moving on.
Idea (a cyst; young and painless means safe), concern (cancer and her children), expectation (to be told it is fine).
Face-to-face examination of both breasts, axillae and supraclavicular nodes with a chaperone offered and recorded; no tests needed before referral.
Cyst, fibroadenoma and other benign causes versus breast cancer; checked skin, nipple and axillary features and lactation.
Recognised that cancer cannot be excluded by age, lack of pain or a benign feel — only by triple assessment.
Unexplained breast lump at 34 meeting the NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway criterion.
Suspected cancer pathway referral today; triple assessment explained; misconceptions corrected; examination with a chaperone and choice of examiner.
Planned around childcare and work; left the door open for any family history she wants to share later.
Chase if no appointment within a week, changes that need sooner contact, result reviewed with her.

social.t: A mother of two young children with a demanding job may struggle to attend a clinic that can take several hours. Planning childcare and time off is part of making the referral work.
Fear of cancer and hospitals is a common reason for delayed presentation and missed appointments. Naming it and pairing honesty with realistic reassurance improves attendance.

legal.t: Explain why a breast examination is needed, get consent, offer a chaperone and record the offer and her response (GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones). She can ask to stop at any time.
An adult with capacity may decline referral. If she did, explain the risk in plain terms, record the discussion, and keep the door open to referral later.

professional.t: Reassuring her to spare distress would fall short of GMC Good medical practice (2024). Be honest, give information in a way she can use, and support her through it.
Track suspected cancer referrals so none are lost, and make sure the result reaches the patient.

community.t: Breast Cancer Now helpline and information on breast clinics; Macmillan Cancer Support if a diagnosis is made.

redFlags: Unexplained breast lump at 30 or over (with or without pain) — suspected cancer pathway referral
Skin changes, a lump in the axilla, or one-sided nipple change
Increase in size since she found it
psychosocial: Two young children — childcare for appointments
ice: Idea: “It’s just a cyst — I’m too young and it doesn’t hurt”
Concern: cancer, and what it would mean for her children
Expectation: to be told it is fine with no fuss

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: An unexplained right breast lump in a 34-year-old woman, possibly enlarging: this meets the NICE NG12 criterion for a suspected cancer pathway referral for triple assessment. The likeliest causes are benign, but that can only be confirmed at the clinic.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “A new lump at your age is usually something harmless like a cyst. But the only way to be sure is a scan at the breast clinic, and at 30 or over we send everyone within two weeks — it’s a check, not a verdict.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me the real fear is what this could mean for your children. That’s exactly why I want you to get a proper answer quickly, not a guess from me.”
management.psychosocial: Plan childcare and time off; offer choice of examiner and a chaperone; encourage her to bring someone to clinic.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway breast referral sent today
Face-to-face examination today with a chaperone
Explain triple assessment and the Faster Diagnosis Standard timescale
safetyNet: Ring if no appointment within a week
Contact sooner if the lump grows or skin or nipple changes appear
GP reviews the result with her

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you apply the NICE NG12 age-30 breast criterion without being talked out of it, while handling a frightened patient kindly. The common fails are clinical collusion and cold delivery.

items.fail: Agreeing it is probably a cyst and reviewing after her next period.
items.why: NICE NG12: an unexplained breast lump at 30 or over is a suspected cancer pathway referral. “Watch and wait” is a management plan not in line with UK practice.
items.fix: State the criterion plainly and refer today, however benign it sounds.

items.fail: Performing or describing an “examination” over video, or letting the planned exam decide whether to refer.
items.why: A breast cannot be examined on a screen, and a benign feel does not remove the referral criterion.
items.fix: Arrange an in-person exam with a chaperone, and say clearly that the referral goes regardless.

items.fail: Taking “just tell me it’s fine” at face value and never exploring the fear.
items.why: Missing the hidden agenda (cancer and her children) forfeits Relating marks and weakens her engagement with the plan.
items.fix: “Can I gently ask what the worry is underneath this?” — then link the answer to the plan.

items.fail: Correcting her myths in a way that frightens her: “Actually, lots of young women get breast cancer.”
items.why: Accurate but alarming delivery drives avoidance.
items.fix: Correct both myths, then balance: most people referred have something harmless.

items.why: Language the patient cannot follow is a standard Global Skills feedback statement.
items.fix: “An examination, a scan and a small needle sample if needed, usually in one visit.”

items.fail: Closing with “you’ll hear from the hospital” and no fail-safe.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no ownership of the result.
items.fix: Chase if no date within a week, named changes to report, and GP follow-up of the result.
